newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU and World Bank say Africa has 'turned the corner'.
newsitem.headline: EU and World Bank say Africa has 'turned the corner'.

text.p: Sub-Saharan African nations may have turned the corner in their bid to get their economies on the right track, European Commission and World Bank officials said on Tuesday.

Joao de Deus Pinheiro, the European development commissioner, told a news conference that more than half the 48 sub-Saharan African nations had shown growth rates of at least five percent in the past two years.
"Clearly there is still much to be done, but this is a positive sign that they are on the right track," said Pinheiro. "Our task is to make sure the train is not derailed."
Pinheiro was speaking after two days of talks in Brussels between the Commission -- the EU's executive -- and the World Bank on cooperation in development in Africa.
World Bank regional vice-president Jean-Louis Sarbib told the same news conference that despite progress, 45 percent of sub-Saharan Africa's population still lived on less than one dollar a day.
"It took a long time for some of these economies to get in the state they are now," he said. "It is going to take a long time for them to fully recover."
The Commission and Bank are currently reviewing progress on cooperation in three African countries they say are taking the right steps to better their economies.

In Mozambique, Ivory Coast and Ethiopia, the two institutions are joining forces to ensure there is no overlap of activity and to help encourage free-market economies after years of central government control.

In these countries the Bank and Commission were working together on projects that focused on job-creation, social development and poverty reduction and were trying to use the fledgling private sector as an engine for growth.
Pinheiro said the Commission and Bank had re-affirmed their desire to focus on 20 African countries whose debt was considered unsustainable.
Sarbib said these so-called "highly indebted poor countries" had a combined debt of $102 billion at the end of 1995.

Pinheiro said the Commission and Bank -- together with donor governments and other organisations -- would make every effort to reduce the debt burden of these three and provide grants to promote economic activity.
"These countries need the possibility of an exit (from debt) strategy", said Pinheiro. "If they can show some mastery over their recourses, we can allow them access to debt reduction facilities."

Sarbib said also that Mozambique, Uganda and Ivory Coast had been identified by the World Bank for special attention as their governments had made it clear they were prepared to make sacrifices to meet targets.

Pinheiro said the Commission and Bank agreed that sustainable economic growth was a key feature in political and social stability -- and vice versa -- and that good governance should be rewarded with financial incentives.
"Over 30 democratic elections have been held (in sub-Saharan Africa) since the beginning of the the nineties," he said. "This is the sort of thing that has to be encouraged, must be encouraged."
